title: Dependency & Supply Chain Hygiene
summary: Treating the dependency tree as part of the attack surface, from lockfiles to automated vulnerability scanning in CI.

slides.markdown:
A modern application typically pulls in hundreds, sometimes thousands, of third-party packages once you count transitive dependencies — packages your dependencies depend on, which you never explicitly chose. Every one of those runs as part of your application with your application's privileges, whether you audited it or not.

That's the entire premise of this topic: **your dependency tree is part of your attack surface**, not a separate concern from your own code. A vulnerability in a package five levels deep in a transitive dependency chain is just as exploitable as one in code your own team wrote — the attacker doesn't care who authored the vulnerable line.

slides.sectionTitle: Your dependency tree is part of your attack surface
slides.markdown:
It's easy to mentally separate "my code" from "library code" and review only the former — but from a security standpoint, that boundary is meaningless. Every dependency you install runs with the same privileges your application has: it can read the same files, make the same network calls, access the same environment variables (including any secrets sitting there), and execute at the same trust level as code you wrote yourself.

The scale makes this a real problem rather than a theoretical one: a typical modern application's `node_modules`, `site-packages`, or equivalent can easily contain **hundreds of packages once transitive dependencies are counted**, most of which no one on the team has ever read a single line of. A vulnerability, or a deliberately malicious package, anywhere in that tree is functionally equivalent to a vulnerability in your own code — same blast radius, same privileges, same access to whatever the application can reach.

slides.subTitle: Reproducibility as a security property
slides.markdown:
A **lockfile** (`package-lock.json`, `poetry.lock`, `Cargo.lock`, and equivalents) records the exact resolved version — often down to a specific hash — of every dependency and transitive dependency in a build, rather than the loose version ranges typically declared in a project's manifest (`^2.1.0`, allowing any compatible 2.x release).

Without a lockfile, two builds run at different times, even from identical source code, can resolve to different actual dependency versions if anything in the range was published in between — including a version that turns out to be compromised. **A lockfile makes reproducibility a security property, not just a convenience one**: the exact same dependency tree gets installed every time, so a build isn't silently exposed to whatever happens to be the newest matching version on the day it runs, and a security review of "what's actually in this build" has one definitive, checkable answer.

The practical discipline: commit the lockfile to version control, and treat any change to it as something to actually look at during code review, not an auto-generated file to ignore — a lockfile diff showing an unexpected new transitive dependency, or a version jump nobody intended, is a real signal worth a second look.

**Software Composition Analysis (SCA)** tools (Dependabot, Snyk, `npm audit`, OWASP Dependency-Check) scan a project's dependency tree against vulnerability databases and flag any package with a known CVE — ideally automatically, on every pull request or on a recurring schedule, rather than something someone has to remember to run manually.

The highest-leverage placement is **in CI, as a gate that can fail a build** for a newly introduced critical vulnerability — the same posture as a failing test — rather than a report someone occasionally glances at in a dashboard. Many SCA tools also support automatically opening a pull request that bumps a vulnerable dependency to a patched version, converting "someone eventually notices and fixes it" into "a fix shows up as a reviewable PR the same day the vulnerability is published or the scanner catches it."

The honest limitation: SCA only catches *known*, publicly disclosed vulnerabilities against the specific package versions in use — it says nothing about an undisclosed vulnerability, and nothing about a package that's technically not vulnerable but is behaviorally malicious (covered next).

slides.sectionTitle: Evaluating a new dependency before adding it
slides.subTitle: Maintenance, popularity, permissions
slides.markdown:
Before adding a new dependency, a few checks catch a meaningful share of future risk, none of which require deep security expertise:

- **Maintenance activity** — recent commits, a maintainer who responds to issues, an active release cadence. An abandoned package accumulates unpatched vulnerabilities forever, because there's no one left to patch them.
- **Popularity and community scrutiny** — a widely-used package has had more eyes on its code, and a compromise is more likely to be noticed quickly by someone else running the same version. This isn't a guarantee (widely-used packages have absolutely been compromised), but it's a real, if imperfect, signal.
- **What it actually needs** — does a date-formatting library need network access or filesystem permissions? A package requesting capabilities disproportionate to its stated purpose is a red flag worth a closer look before adding it, not after.
- **Transitive weight** — how many *additional* packages does adding this one pull in? A single new direct dependency that drags in forty transitive ones has forty times the attack surface of the number it appears to add.

None of these checks are foolproof individually, but skipping all of them — adding whatever package shows up first in a search, with zero review — is how a large share of real supply-chain incidents start.

slides.sectionTitle: A known-CVE direct dependency vs the same CVE in a transitive one
slides.markdown:
| | Known CVE in a direct dependency | Same CVE in a transitive dependency |
|---|---|---|
| Visibility | Shows up in your manifest file directly | Buried several levels deep; often unknown to the team until a scanner flags it |
| Fix path | Update the version pin directly in your manifest | May require waiting for an intermediate dependency to update its own dependency first, or overriding the transitive version manually |
| Team awareness | The team chose this package and presumably knows it exists | The team may never have heard of the vulnerable package at all |
| Realistic timeline to fix | Often same-day, a version bump and a deploy | Can be blocked on an upstream maintainer's own release cadence, sometimes weeks |

The transitive case is why SCA tooling matters more than manual review: no one is going to manually audit a dependency tree hundreds of packages deep to notice a CVE in something three levels removed from anything they chose. It's also why some ecosystems support **dependency overrides/resolutions** — forcing a specific transitive package to a patched version even before the intermediate dependency that pulls it in has updated its own declared requirement — as a stopgap while waiting for the proper upstream fix to propagate.

slides.sectionTitle: Beyond CVEs: malicious and compromised packages
slides.subTitle: The senior-level nuance
slides.markdown:
SCA tooling protects against *known, disclosed* vulnerabilities — but a growing and distinct category of supply-chain risk is a package that's **deliberately malicious**, either from the start or after a legitimate maintainer's account or publishing credentials are compromised. There's no CVE for this, because it's not a coding mistake — it's intentional, and it typically ships in a routine-looking version bump that most automated scanning won't flag as anything unusual until well after the fact.

Real incidents in this category have looked like: a popular package's maintainer account gets compromised via a phished credential, and a malicious version is published that exfiltrates environment variables or installs a backdoor, distributed to everyone who happens to update during the exposure window. Others have involved a maintainer intentionally shipping malicious code into a widely-used package after a dispute, or a **typosquatting** package (a name one character off from a popular package, e.g. `reqeusts` instead of `requests`) that a developer installs by a simple typo.

The mitigations that help here are different from SCA: pinning exact versions via a lockfile (so an update doesn't silently pull in a newly-compromised release without a deliberate, reviewed version bump), being deliberate about *which* packages get auto-updated versus manually reviewed, and treating an unexpected new transitive dependency or an unusual version jump in a lockfile diff as worth a second look, not routine noise.

slides.sectionTitle: Numbers: how much of a modern app is someone else's code
slides.markdown:
It's genuinely common for **70-90% or more of the executable code in a modern web or mobile application to come from third-party dependencies** rather than code the team itself wrote — a modest number of direct dependencies routinely balloons into hundreds of packages once every transitive dependency is counted.

That ratio reframes what "reviewing your codebase" actually means: a team that reviews every line of its own code carefully but never looks at its dependency tree has reviewed a small minority of what's actually running in production. This is the practical justification for automated SCA scanning being non-negotiable rather than optional — manual review simply cannot scale to a dependency tree that size, and the vast majority of the code executing under your application's identity was written, and is maintained (or isn't), by people outside your organization entirely.

slides.sectionTitle: Force-updating every dependency right before a release
slides.markdown:
The pitfall, common enough to have a familiar shape: someone runs a blanket "update all dependencies to latest" command shortly before a release — sometimes specifically *because* it's near a release and there's a sense of wanting everything current before shipping — pulling in whatever the newest version of every package happens to be, with no individual review of what changed in any of them.

This inverts the actual risk calculus. Right before a release is exactly the **worst** time to introduce unreviewed changes across dozens of dependencies at once: there's minimal time to catch a behavioral regression, a newly introduced vulnerability, or (in the rare but real worst case) a compromised release, before it ships to production. It also makes root-causing any resulting issue much harder — a bug that appears after updating forty packages simultaneously could be caused by any one of them, or an interaction between several.

The healthier pattern: dependency updates on a **regular, boring cadence** well ahead of any release deadline, ideally automated (a bot opening one PR per update) and reviewed individually rather than in one large batch — so any single update that causes a problem is easy to isolate and revert, and there's actual time to notice a problem before it's under release-deadline pressure to ship anyway.
